summary: This episode continues the story of the six Yathrib youths who met the Prophet ﷺ at Mina, treating them as the founders of Madinah, and follows how they returned, taught their families and tribes, and how six became twelve at the first Pledge of Aqabah. The ustaz explains Madinah's background of weariness after the Battle of Bu'ath, the Jewish neighbours awaiting the final prophet, and the soft-heartedness of the Aws and Khazraj, and stresses building the foundation from the home, grounded in evidence, networks and narrative. He then goes through the six points of the pledge, also known as the women's pledge: no shirk, no stealing, no adultery, no killing of children, no slander and no disobedience in what is right, and ties them to our families today. The ustaz mentions the book The Obstacle Is the Way, that the obstacle is the path, and closes with a teaser about the two teachers sent to Madinah.
keyPoints: The six Yathrib youths were the founders of Madinah, and Aisha RA said Allah arranged the Battle of Bu'ath before the Prophet's ﷺ coming.
The Aws and Khazraj, living beside the Jews, understood the concept of prophethood, and the Jews' threat to expel them in fact prepared them to welcome the Prophet.
The six youths honestly admitted their society's problem, saw Islam as a comprehensive solution, and did not ask the Prophet to come at once because they knew a foundation had to be built first.

Building a foundation starts at home, then rests on Quran and sunnah evidence, then spreads through family and tribal networks, and finally through a narrative that gives people the imagination of a solution.
The first Pledge of Aqabah took place in the 12th year of da'wah with twelve people, and is called the women's pledge because it had no war clause.
The six points of the pledge: no shirk, no stealing, no adultery, no killing of children, no slander, and no disobedience in what is right.
The obstacle is the path: the Prophet ﷺ met obstacle after obstacle yet never stopped, and the prophets are tested the most.

lessons.title: Young people who care about their society
lessons.body: The six youths did not live like zombies addicted to social media; they saw a sick society and looked for a solution.

lessons.title: Be honest in admitting problems
lessons.body: We can solve a problem only if we admit it is a problem, and many problems remain because we do not accept them as problems.

lessons.title: Patience in building the foundation, no rushing
lessons.body: The youths did not ask the Prophet to come at once because they knew groundwork was needed, and seniors can give perspective to young people in a hurry.

lessons.title: Start from home
lessons.body: The first step of building a project is the home, because the family is the basis of society and the first place to convey.

lessons.title: Da'wah must rest on evidence
lessons.body: There must be 'Allah said' and 'the Messenger said'; personal opinion cannot come ahead of revelation.

lessons.title: Give people the imagination of a solution
lessons.body: Talking only about problems is not enough; a narrative that shows the way out makes the message sink in.

lessons.title: The obstacle is the path
lessons.body: The Prophet and the prophets met the most obstacles yet did not stop; obstacles are the process of growth.

lessons.title: Change people first, before rules
lessons.body: The first pledge had no clause on war or Hijra; the verses of rulings came mostly in Madinah after people were built.

lessons.title: Give children room to ask
lessons.body: When children ask hard questions we cannot answer, say let's find the answer together; the home is the place for clarity of faith.

lessons.title: Don't hand over a child's religion to institutions alone
lessons.body: Children live in two worlds when school teaches religion but home does not practise it; parents remain responsible.

lessons.title: Protect people's honour, hold your fingers and tongue
lessons.body: When news arrives that damages someone's honour, keep quiet and do not spread it; a Muslim's honour is very great with Allah.

lessons.title: Learn to be a good follower
lessons.body: We love discussing leadership but forget followership; families and organisations shake when leadership is not accepted.

glossary.meaning: The war between the Aws and Khazraj before the Hijra that weakened Madinah's leaders.
A solid foundation; the method of building the base before the building, including in da'wah and knowledge.
The pledge of allegiance between the Prophet and the people of Yathrib at Aqabah, Mina.
A leader appointed to organise and oversee his people after the pledge.
Protection of religion, one of the basic aims of the Shariah, which the ustaz links to forbidding shirk.
The ability to be a good follower, which the ustaz says is rarely discussed compared with leadership.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions this hadith in Sahih Bukhari as Allah's preparation before the Prophet was accepted in Madinah.
dalil.translation: Aisha RA said that the day of Bu'ath was a day Allah brought forward for His Messenger ﷺ, so that when he arrived in Madinah their nobles had split and been killed.

dalil.context: They recognised a book confirming what they had, and had earlier prayed for victory through the Prophet's coming, but when he came they denied it out of ego.
dalil.translation: When a Scripture came to them from God confirming what they already had, and when they had been praying for victory against the disbelievers, even when there came to them something they knew [to be true], they disbelieved in it: God rejects those who disbelieve.

dalil.context: Hold fast to Allah's rope and remember the blessing when you were enemies and Allah united your hearts; exegetes such as Ibn Kathir link it to the Aws and Khazraj.
dalil.translation: Hold fast to God’s rope all together; do not split into factions. Remember God’s favour to you: you were enemies and then He brought your hearts together and you became brothers by His grace; you were about to fall into a pit of Fire and He saved you from it- in this way God makes His revelations clear to you so that you may be rightly guided.

dalil.context: The ustaz reads the verse that Allah created spouses so that you find tranquillity, and links it to the family as the base of society. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Another of His signs is that He created spouses from among yourselves for you to live with in tranquillity: He ordained love and kindness between you. There truly are signs in this for those who reflect.

dalil.context: The ustaz says this hadith is narrated by Imam Ahmad and graded hasan by hadith scholars, and explains that Jabir may be one of the six.
dalil.translation: Jabir RA narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed in Mecca ten years going to people at their lodgings, asking who would give protection until he conveyed the message, and for him Paradise; then Allah sent them from Yathrib, and there was no Ansar house without Muslims.

dalil.context: The ustaz says do not go ahead of Allah and His Messenger, as the principle that da'wah must rest on evidence. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Believers, do not push yourselves forward in the presence of God and His Messenger––be mindful of God: He hears and knows all––

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it as a saying not confirmed as a hadith, and links it to the wisdom in the book The Obstacle Is the Way.
dalil.translation: Wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he has more right to it.

dalil.context: The ustaz stresses that we are not asked to request trials, but when they come we put them in perspective.
dalil.translation: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked who is tested most severely, and the Prophet ﷺ replied the prophets, then those most like them, and so on; a person is tested according to his religion, and trials keep afflicting him until he walks on earth without sin.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it to show that only believers can appreciate obstacles as good.
dalil.translation: How wonderful is the affair of the believer; all of it is good for him, if given a blessing he is grateful and if afflicted he is patient.

dalil.context: The ustaz reads the translation of the hadith in Al-Bukhari's Kitab al-Iman and Sahih Muslim; Ubadah was one of the naqibs on the night of Aqabah.
dalil.translation: Ubadah ibn Samit narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said pledge to me that you will not associate anything with Allah, not steal, not commit adultery, not kill your children, not bring a slander you invent, and not disobey in what is right; whoever fulfils it, his reward is with Allah, whoever violates something and is punished in this world, that is expiation, and whoever Allah conceals, his matter is with Allah.

dalil.context: The ustaz says if you commit shirk, your deeds will be void. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: It has already been revealed to you [Prophet] and to those before you: ‘If you ascribe any partner to God, all your work will come to nothing: you will be one if the losers.

dalil.context: The verse that gives the details of this pledge, and scholars differ on whether it refers to the first Aqabah or the pledge with women in Madinah.
dalil.translation: Prophet, when believing women come and pledge to you that they will not ascribe any partner to God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children, nor lie about who has fathered their children, nor disobey you in any righteous thing, then you should accept their pledge of allegiance and pray to God to forgive them: God is most forgiving and merciful.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it to explain why verses of rulings came mostly in Madinah after people were built first.
dalil.translation: Aisha RA said if an absolute prohibition had come at the start no one could have given it up, but because there was a process, when the prohibition came the Companions gave it up at once.

dalil.context: The ustaz refers to the principle in Surah An-Nur when news arrives that damages honour, which is to say this is a lie, and Abu Ayyub's reply to his wife. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: When you heard the lie, why did believing men and women not think well of their own people and declare, ‘This is obviously a lie’?

dalil.context: Maryam AS feared having her honour shamed more than death and said would that she had died before this. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: and, when the pains of childbirth drove her to [cling to] the trunk of a palm tree, she exclaimed, ‘I wish I had been dead and forgotten long before all this!’

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it while advising us to keep quiet when news arrives that shames someone's honour.
dalil.translation: Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is leaving what does not concern him.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions that tearing down someone's honour is worse than tearing down the Kaaba.
dalil.translation: The sanctity of a Muslim's honour is greater than the Kaaba.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions the verse of obeying Allah, the Messenger and those in authority as the basis of followership. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: You who believe, obey God and the Messenger, and those in authority among you. If you are in dispute over any matter, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day: that is better and fairer in the end.
